text:
Malavaggo

250 For whom this <note>greed or attachment</note> is cut off, uprooted, and removed, he indeed attains concentration whether by day or by night. <note>8. The story of Tissa the novice, III, 357</note>

251 There is no fire like lust, there is no grip like hatred, there is no net like delusion, there is no river like craving. <note>9. The story of the five lay followers, III, 360</note>

252 It is easy to see the faults of others, but one's own are difficult to see. One winnows the faults of others like chaff, but covers one's own as a crafty gambler hides a losing die. <note>10. The story of Meṇḍaka the treasurer, III, 363</note>

253 For one who sees only the faults of others, and who is always irritable, the <term>āsavas</term> <gloss>mental taints or intoxicants</gloss> increase; he is far from the destruction of these taints. <note>11. The story of the monk who was always finding fault, III, 376</note>

254 There is no footprint in the sky, and there is no ascetic outside <note>of the Buddha's teaching</note>. Living beings delight in proliferation <note>of mental fabrications</note>, but the <term>Tathāgatas</term> <gloss>those who have attained the truth</gloss> are without proliferation.

255 There is no footprint in the sky, and there is no ascetic outside. There are no eternal compounded things, and there is no agitation for the Buddhas. <note>12. The story of Subhadda the wanderer, III, 377</note>

XVIII THE CHAPTER ON IMPURITIES (MALAVAGGO) THE EIGHTEENTH

---

1 Bṝ kaḷi va 2 F ca Bṝ va
3 K F bāhiro, Bṝ, Sḝ bāhire

252 Jāt III 223

<summary>This page contains verses 250 through 255 of the Malavaggo, covering themes of mental concentration, the dangers of lust and hatred, the difficulty of self-reflection, and the nature of the Buddha's state.</summary>
